impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not govern prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct, and whether a reference patent may receive the filing date of an earlier provisional application without satisfying Dynamic Drinkware's requirement that at least one claim be supported by the provisional's written description.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing the critical question of how to determine the effective prior art date of a patent reference under AIA § 102(d)(2) when the reference claims priority to a provisional application. The court's resolution of the tension between Dynamic Drinkware and the Board's Penumbra framework has broad implications for IPR proceedings and patent validity challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially stricter standard for establishing the prior art date of reference patents, making it harder for IPR petitioners to rely on provisional filing dates to invalidate patents under the AIA.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty using reference patents as prior art when those references rely on provisional application filing dates for their effective date.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how to apply the Alice/Mayo framework to claims involving optimized data tables used in digital communications.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL of non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award. The split decision on eligibility across related patents provides important guidance on how § 101 applies to communications technology patents involving mathematical optimization.
impacts.positiveImplications: The affirmance of eligibility for some claims and the damages award supports patent holders in the communications technology space, reinforcing that claims tied to specific technical implementations can survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur of eligibility for other claims signals ongoing uncertainty for companies holding patents that may be characterized as claiming abstract mathematical concepts, even when applied to specific technological fields like digital broadcasting.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered a contractual termination provision.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights and did not terminate when TexasLDPC shifted to patent enforcement. This clarifies when an exclusive licensee has standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees gain clarity that shifting business operations to enforcement does not necessarily terminate a license agreement, and that a well-drafted exclusive license can confer standing to sue independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense: they cannot easily challenge standing by arguing that a licensee's pivot to enforcement activities constitutes a cessation of business operations that terminates the license.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' where the dispute is fundamentally one of contract interpretation under state law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent litigation settlement agreement and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. The court determined that interpreting whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination was a state-law contract question, not a patent law question conferring Federal Circuit jurisdiction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on jurisdictional boundaries, allowing parties to patent settlement agreements to litigate contract disputes in regional circuits where they may receive more favorable treatment on state-law contract issues.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates jurisdictional uncertainty for parties drafting patent settlement agreements with contingent payment terms, as disputes over such terms may not be heard by the patent-specialist Federal Circuit.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court may assess copyright infringement damages against the government via a hypothetical negotiation rather than deferring to existing license agreement terms, and what constitutes the proper application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in calculating damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to use a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA software, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the book of wisdom and assessed non-compensatory damages. This provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government contract disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's affirmation that hypothetical negotiation is a permissible damages methodology even when a prior license agreement exists, potentially yielding higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The vacatur regarding the book of wisdom and non-compensatory damages imposes limits on copyright holders' ability to inflate damages calculations beyond what is compensatory, requiring more rigorous damages proof.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's design patent infringement framework under Egyptian Goddess improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions that should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The en banc Federal Circuit denied rehearing in a design patent case, with a notable dissent from Chief Judge Moore arguing that the Egyptian Goddess framework has been misapplied to improperly resolve infringement at summary judgment based on differences rather than overall similarity. The split decision leaves the current design patent infringement standard intact but signals significant internal disagreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the continued application of the Egyptian Goddess framework, which allows courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment when claimed and accused designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that district courts may resolve infringement at summary judgment based on differences alone, without full consideration of the ordinary observer test or prior art context, potentially undervaluing design patent rights.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' between a provisional application and a non-provisional patent constituted correction of an obvious typographical error that preserved the patent's priority date, or instead introduced new matter that broke the priority chain.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's patent covering compounds related to Pfizer's Paxlovid® COVID-19 treatment, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error. Because the patent could not claim priority to the earlier provisional, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated all claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical companies benefit from a strict standard for claiming priority to provisional applications, ensuring that changes to chemical definitions between provisional and non-provisional filings can break the priority chain and expose patents to prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face significant risk from even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications, as the court's strict approach to the 'obvious error' correction doctrine may invalidate patents covering commercially valuable drug compounds.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a prior art reference anticipated the asserted claims of a patent directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants, and whether the accused drug-eluting coronary stent systems infringed those claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of the patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stents. The decision eliminated a damages award against BSC.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the court's willingness to overturn jury verdicts on invalidity and non-infringement as a matter of law, providing a check against potentially unsupported patent infringement verdicts in the medical device space.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and patent assertion entities face risk that infringement verdicts supported by jury findings may be reversed on appeal, potentially undermining the value of patents in the drug-eluting stent and medical implant technology areas.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation to encompass salt forms of those compounds, and whether the court properly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement. The claim construction holding that 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' encompass their salt forms is significant for Hatch-Waxman pharmaceutical patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmed claim construction and injunction, maintaining market exclusivity for Nuedexta against generic competition through the patent's expiration date.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face barriers to market entry when courts construe drug compound terms broadly to encompass salt forms, and the vacatur of the bond waiver signals that courts must impose meaningful financial protections for enjoined parties.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to equitable tolling under the American Pipe class action tolling rule.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's statute of limitations is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities. This eliminates class action tolling as a mechanism for preserving late-filed claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government benefits from a firm limitations period that cannot be extended by class action tolling, providing certainty and finality for claims involving government-sponsored enterprise investments and other financial disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with claims against the government lose the ability to rely on American Pipe tolling to extend the filing deadline, requiring strict adherence to the six-year limitations period even when a related class action is pending.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in a sunset review of antidumping duty orders within 15 days of initiation conflicts with the Tariff Act, which imposes no express deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and upheld Commerce's 15-day regulatory deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders. The court found the regulation was a permissible exercise of agency authority where the statute was silent on timing, preserving Commerce's ability to efficiently administer the sunset review process.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the preservation of Commerce's structured sunset review process, which ensures timely review of antidumping duty orders that protect against unfairly priced imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign exporters and importers face the continued burden of Commerce's regulatory deadlines in sunset reviews, with the 15-day participation window remaining enforceable despite the statute's silence on timing.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint against Volkswagen without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The decision reinforces that courts may impose fees and sanctions on patent plaintiffs and their attorneys who pursue meritless infringement claims with inadequate factual basis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the robust enforcement of § 285 fee-shifting and attorney sanctions provisions, deterring meritless patent infringement suits and compensating defendants for defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face heightened risk of fee awards and personal sanctions when pursuing cases with insufficient factual foundation, particularly where pre-suit investigation is inadequate.

impacts.caseName: Ridge Corp. v. Kirk NationaLease Co.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted a preliminary injunction against alleged infringers of a patent directed to insulated overhead doors, considering likelihood of success on the merits and the balance of equities.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of a preliminary injunction in a patent infringement case involving insulated overhead door technology and remanded for further proceedings. The decision addresses the standards for preliminary injunctive relief in patent cases, including the requirements for demonstrating likelihood of success on infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to reverse preliminary injunctions that do not meet the rigorous standards for likelihood of success on the merits in patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders seeking to enjoin competitors from the market during litigation face a higher bar for obtaining preliminary relief, potentially allowing competitors to continue selling accused products during protracted patent proceedings.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court that has already concluded venue is improper may also reach the merits and dismiss on patent eligibility grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the same order.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, holding that the court did not err in reaching the § 101 merits after finding venue improper. The e-commerce patent at issue was found ineligible. The case also involved an automatic stay as to a co-defendant Big Lots that had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from courts' ability to dismiss on multiple grounds simultaneously, including patent ineligibility, even when venue is also found to be improper—providing broader preclusive effect against future filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk adverse rulings on the merits of patent eligibility even in cases where venue is clearly improper, potentially establishing precedent that undermines their patent's validity across all jurisdictions.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted patent claims covering crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salts satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), where the specification discloses both crystalline and amorphous forms of the salt.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that Exelixis's patents covering cabozantinib malate salt forms (the active ingredient in Cabometyx® cancer drug) have adequate written description, upholding the district court's finding against MSN's invalidity challenge in this Hatch-Waxman litigation. The decision protects Exelixis's patent portfolio covering a commercially significant oncology drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the court's affirmation that written description requirements can be met even where specifications disclose multiple forms (crystalline and amorphous), supporting broad patent protection for valuable drug compounds.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face continued barriers to entry for cabozantinib malate products, as the court's ruling validates the patent protection strategy of claiming specific crystalline salt forms of known drug compounds.
